en: Bret, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
zh: Bret，非常感谢你来到这里，欢迎收听这期播客。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks for having me.
zh: 谢谢你的邀请。

speaker: Unknown
en: My pleasure.
zh: 这是我的荣幸。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's so much that I want to talk about.
zh: 我有很多想谈论的话题。

speaker: Unknown
en: You've done so many incredible things over the course of your career.
zh: 在你的职业生涯中，你做了这么多令人难以置信的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: Just boggles the mind, the things that you've done, and we're going to talk about a lot of that sort of stuff, but I want to actually start with the opposite.
zh: 你所做的一切真让人费解，我们将会谈论很多这类事情，但我实际上想从相反的一面开始。

speaker: Unknown
en: I want to talk about a time that you messed up, a time that you screwed up in a big way.
zh: 我想谈谈你搞砸的一次经历，一次你犯下大错的时候。

speaker: Unknown
en: We have this recurring segment on the podcast called Fail Corner, and so, I thought it'd be fun to just start there before we get into all the great stuff you've done.
zh: 我们在播客上有一个常设环节叫“失败角”，所以，我想在进入你做过的所有伟大的事情之前，从那里开始会很有趣。

speaker: Unknown
en: What's a story that comes to mind when you think about maybe your biggest mistake in building a product?
zh: 当你想到你在构建产品时可能犯过的最大错误时，想到了什么故事？

speaker: Unknown
en: It may not be the biggest, but it was my first prominent mistake as a product manager at Google.
zh: 这可能不是最大的，但那是我在 Google 担任产品经理时第一次显眼的错误。

speaker: Unknown
en: So for me, it feels big because it was very formative for me as a product designer.
zh: 所以对我来说，它感觉很大，因为那对我来说，作为一名产品设计师是非常具有塑造意义的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I joined Google in late 2002, early 2003, and I was one of the earliest associate product managers at the company and first, was working on the search system, essentially expanding our index from 1 billion webpages to 10 billion, which was a big deal at the time.
zh: 所以我在 2002 年末、2003 年初加入 Google，我是公司最早的一批副产品经理之一，首先从事的是搜索系统的工作，主要是将我们的索引从 10 亿个网页扩展到 100 亿个，这在当时是一件大事。

speaker: Unknown
en: It seems quaint now.
zh: 现在看来这显得很小。

speaker: Unknown
en: Then I did a decent job and so my boss, Marissa Meyer, gave me the opportunity to lead a new product initiative, which was a big bet on me and it was both an opportunity to do something for Google, but I was also being pretty scrutinized just as a young new product manager and the premise given to me was work on local search.
zh: 然后我做得还不错，所以我的老板 Marissa Mayer 给了我机会去领导一个新的产品计划，这对我来说是一个巨大的赌注，这既是为 Google 做点事情的机会，但作为一个年轻的新产品经理，我也受到了相当严格的审视，给我的前提是做本地搜索。

speaker: Unknown
en: At the time, the Yellow Pages was still dominant and well, Google was really good at searching the web.
zh: 在当时，黄页仍然占据主导地位，而且 Google 非常擅长搜索网页。

speaker: Unknown
en: It wasn't really good for finding a plumber or a restaurant just because it wasn't really a huge part of the internet at the time.
zh: 它并不擅长寻找水管工或餐厅，仅仅是因为这并不是当时互联网的很大一部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: So this content wasn't necessarily on the internet and even if it was, you didn't really want to find plumbers in Manhattan, you wanted to find plumbers in San Francisco, if you're me.
zh: 所以这些内容不一定在互联网上，即使是在，你也不一定想在曼哈顿找水管工，如果你是我的话，你想在旧金山找水管工。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it was both a technical problem and a product problem and a content problem.
zh: 所以这既是一个技术问题，也是一个产品问题和内容问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: We launched the first version of that product that I was the product manager for, was called Google Local and it was, I'll be a little bit more critical now than I might've been at the time, but it was a little bit of a me too version of Yahoo Yellow Pages, essentially grafting on Yellow Pages search on top of Google Search and with a properly crafted query you could see those listings at the top of your search results but a standalone site at local.google.com.
zh: 我们推出了该产品的第一个版本，我是该产品的产品经理，它叫 Google Local，我现在可能会比当时更批判一点，但它有点像是 Yahoo 黄页的“我也是”版本，本质上是在 Google 搜索之上嫁接黄页搜索，如果你有一个精心设计的查询，你可以在搜索结果的顶部看到这些列表，但在 local.google.com 上有一个独立的网站。

speaker: Unknown
en: Actually, it was an important enough initiative that actually, there was on the Google homepage, it had Web, Images and Local was up there as well, so it's got top bill.
zh: 实际上，这是一个足够重要的计划，实际上，在 Google 首页上，它有 Web、Images 和 Local 也在那里，所以它得到了顶级的版面。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean you could put almost any link on the Google homepage and get a lot of traffic to it.
zh: 我的意思是，你几乎可以在 Google 首页放任何链接，并从中获得大量流量。

speaker: Unknown
en: And despite that, it didn't do that well and to not do that well with a link from the Google homepage is embarrassing.
zh: 尽管如此，它的表现并不好，作为一个来自 Google 首页的链接却表现不好，这很尴尬。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's not much one can do more than giving you that kind of traffic to give you an add that as a product leader or a product manager.
zh: 作为一个产品领导者或产品经理，除了给你那种流量之外，人们做不了太多事情来给你提供更多。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the product was fine, it worked, but it really wasn't differentiated.
zh: 那个产品还可以，能用，但它真的没有差异化。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in many ways, I think, again, I think I've had these reflections more sense than at the time, that I had some of the time, but why use this instead of Yahoo Yellow Pages?
zh: 而且在很多方面，我想，再次，我认为我现在比当时进行了更多的思考，那我为什么要用这个而不是 Yahoo 黄页？

speaker: Unknown
en: But more than anything else, why use this instead of the Yellow Pages?
zh: 但最重要的是，为什么要用这个而不是黄页？

speaker: Unknown
en: It was a digital version of something that had come before.
zh: 它是对以前事物的数字化版本。

speaker: Unknown
en: Had a pretty tough product review with Marissa and Larry and others and it was fine.
zh: 我和 Marissa 以及 Larry 和其他人进行了一次相当艰难的产品评审，那还可以。

speaker: Unknown
en: I wasn't about to get fired or something, but it was, I don't know, the shine on my reputation was waning a little bit.
zh: 我不会被解雇什么的，但我不知道，我声誉的光环正在消退一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: And they gave me another shot to do a V2 of it and I got the impression it wasn't like my last shot, but I certainly was feeling a little dejected from going from a hot shot, new PM to a new thing.
zh: 他们给了我另一次机会去做它的 V2 版本，我的印象是这不像是我的最后一次机会，但我肯定感到有点沮丧，从一个炙手可热的新 PM 变成做一件新事物。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, we spent a lot of time thinking about how can you make something that's just much more compelling and not just a digital version of the Yellow Pages and not just so similar to some of the other products out there.
zh: 所以，我们花了很多时间思考如何制造出更有吸引力的东西，而不仅仅是黄页的数字化版本，也不仅仅与市面上的其他产品如此相似。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that ended up being the thread that we pulled that resulted in Google Maps.
zh: 这最终成为了我们拉扯的那条线，结果导致了 Google Maps。

speaker: Unknown
en: We had licensed from MapQuest, the ability to put this little map next to the search results, it was always the ugliest part of the product and we always made these backhanded comments about it internally and we spent a lot of time saying, what if we inverted the hierarchy here and made the map the canvas?
zh: 我们从 MapQuest 获得了授权，能够在搜索结果旁边放一小块地图，它总是产品中最丑的部分，我们总是在内部对它做出些含沙射影的评论，我们花了很多时间说，如果我们在这里反转层级结构，把地图作为画布会怎么样？

speaker: Unknown
en: We ended up finding Lars and Jens Rasmussen who had been working on this Windows mapping product and we got them into the company and started exploring this space and it ended up where, through that exploration we ended up integrating a lot of different products.
zh: 我们最终找到了 Lars 和 Jens Rasmussen 兄弟，他们一直在做这个 Windows 地图产品，我们把他们招进了公司并开始探索这个领域，最终结果是，通过那次探索，我们最终整合了许多不同的产品。

speaker: Unknown
en: We ended up integrating mapping local search, driving directions, like all of these products at the time were actually separate product categories and ended up with something that redefined the industry and certainly my career.
zh: 我们最终整合了地图本地搜索、驾驶路线，像当时所有的这些产品实际上是独立的产品类别，最终得到了某种重新定义了行业的东西，当然也重新定义了我的职业生涯。

speaker: Unknown
en: But it took, I think for me as a product leader, it changed the way I think about product just because there's feature and functionality and then there's like why should I use this thing in the first place?
zh: 但是花了一点时间，我认为对我来说作为产品领导者，它改变了我对产品的看法，因为这里有特性和功能，然后还有像“我为什么要首先使用这个东西？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was notable, there was a couple of interesting moments.
zh: 这一点很值得注意，有几个有趣的时刻。

speaker: Unknown
en: When we launched Google Maps we got about 10 million people using it on the first day, which at that scale of the internet at the time was huge.
zh: 当我们推出 Google Maps 时，第一天大约有 1000 万人在使用它，就当时互联网的规模而言，这是巨大的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then in August of 2005, we integrated satellite imagery from a recent acquisition called Keyhole, which became Google Earth and we got 90 million people using it on the same day.
zh: 然后在 2005 年 8 月，我们整合了来自最近收购的名为 Keyhole 的卫星图像，它成为了 Google Earth，同一天有 9000 万人在使用它。

speaker: Unknown
en: Everyone wanted to look at the top of their house when the imagery came out.
zh: 当图像发布时，每个人都想看他们家的屋顶。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was really interesting because there's so many subtle product lessons in there.
zh: 这真的很有趣，因为那里有很多微妙的产品教训。

speaker: Unknown
en: First is, I think as you have these new technologies, rather than literally digitizing what came before, if you can create an entirely new experience, it answers the question for a new customer, why should I give this the time of day?
zh: 首先，我认为当你拥有这些新技术时，与其字面地将以前的事物数字化，如果你能创造一种全新的体验，它就能为一个新客户回答这个问题，我为什么要花时间在这上面？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, really disassembling the Lego set and reassembling into something new rather than just digitizing what was there before.
zh: 所以，真正拆开乐高积木并重新组装成新的东西，而不仅仅是数字化以前存在的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: Certainly, that was the lesson I think in Google Maps, really was native to the platform in a way that a paper map couldn't be and that was a really meaningful breakthrough.
zh: 当然，这就是我想在 Google Maps 中得到的教训，它真的以某种方式原生于平台，这是纸质地图无法做到的，那是一个真正有意义的突破。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then with satellite imagery, it honestly wasn't the most important part of Google Maps, but it was the sizzle to the steak and it created, I don't think the term viral was a thing people said back then, but it created a viral moment.
zh: 然后有了卫星图像，老实说，它并不是 Google Maps 最重要的一部分，但它是牛排上的滋滋声，它创造了一种，我想“病毒式传播”这个词当时人们还不怎么说的，但它创造了一个病毒式时刻。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were on Saturday Night Live, which is the coolest thing.
zh: 我们上了《周六夜现场》，那是很酷的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: Andy Samberg in, I think it was called Lazy Sunday rapped about Google Maps and Lars and I were texting each other.
zh: Andy Samberg 在，我想那首歌叫《Lazy Sunday》里唱到了 Google Maps，Lars 和我当时在互发短信。

speaker: Unknown
en: We did it.
zh: 我们做到了。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're on Saturday Live.
zh: 我们是在《Saturday Live》上。

speaker: Unknown
en: Mission accomplished.
zh: 任务完成。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was also showing that as you're there thinking about products, there's the why you decide to use a product and then what is the enduring value.
zh: 而且这也表明了，当你在那里思考产品时，有这样一个原因，就是你决定使用一个产品，然后什么是持久的价值。

speaker: Unknown
en: And those are deeply related but not all the same thing.
zh: 而且这些是深度相关的，但并不是同一回事。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I just learned so many lessons that I took with me for every subsequent product that I worked on.
zh: 我学到了太多的教训，我把这些教训带入了我在随后从事的每一个产品中。

speaker: Unknown
en: That is an awesome story.
zh: 那是一个很棒的故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: One I think it's really empowering for people to hear, even you Bret, who I'm going to share all the successes you've had, have had a massive failure with the CEO of Google [inaudible 00:11:30] just like Bret, you screwed up.
zh: 首先，我认为这对人们来说真的很受鼓舞，即使是你 Bret，虽然我要分享你取得的所有成功，但也曾和谷歌首席执行官一起遭遇过巨大的失败 [听不清 00:11:30]，就像 Bret 一样，你搞砸了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was such a big bet.
zh: 而且那是一次巨大的赌注。

speaker: Unknown
en: So one, just it's possible to succeed as you have succeeded in spite of a massive failure like this.
zh: 所以第一，尽管有这样的巨大失败，像你取得的成功那样获得成功是可能的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then some of the product lessons you shared, just to highlight a few of these things because I think this is great, is just you will often not win if you just make something that's a better copy of something else, what you want to look for is something that is an entirely new experience, something that's differentiated, something that's a lot more compelling.
zh: 然后你分享的一些产品教训，只是为了强调其中的几件事，因为我认为这很棒，就是如果你只是制作某种更好的、对其他东西的复制品，你通常不会赢，你要寻找的是一种全新的体验，某种有差异化的东西，某种更具吸引力的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: Let's flip to talk about what you've learned from actually being very successful at a lot of things.
zh: 让我们转而谈谈你从在许多事情上非常成功中学到了什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I was looking at your resume and you basically have been very successful at every level of the career ladder and in such a huge variety of roles.
zh: 所以我看了你的简历，你基本上在职业阶梯的每个层面都非常成功，而且在如此多种不同的角色中。

speaker: Unknown
en: So let me just read a few of these things for folks that aren't super familiar with your background.
zh: 所以让我为那些不太熟悉你背景的人读其中的一些事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: You were CTO of Meta, you were co-CEO of Salesforce, you're also CPO and COO at Salesforce.
zh: 你是 Meta 的 CTO，你是 Salesforce 的联席 CEO，你也是 Salesforce 的 CPO 和 COO。

speaker: Unknown
en: At Google, you joined as an associate product manager where you famously, you didn't mention this but you rebuilt Google Maps on weekend.
zh: 在谷歌，你以助理产品经理的身份加入，你著名的——你没有提到这一点——你在周末重建了谷歌地图。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're not going to talk about that.
zh: 我们不打算谈论那个。

speaker: Unknown
en: You're chairman of the board at OpenAI.
zh: 你是 OpenAI 董事会主席。

speaker: Unknown
en: You were chairman of the board at Twitter.
zh: 你是 Twitter 董事会主席。

speaker: Unknown
en: You've also founded three different companies, one social network, one productivity docs company called Quip, and now, Sierra.
zh: 你还创立了三家不同的公司，一家社交网络，一家生产力文档公司叫 Quip，以及现在的 Sierra。

speaker: Unknown
en: Fun fact, at FriendFeed you invented the like button and I don't know if people know that and also just the newsfeed, I'll just throw that out there to give you some credit.
zh: 有趣的事实，在 FriendFeed 你发明了点赞按钮，我不知道人们是否知道这一点，还有信息流，我就顺便提一下，给你一些肯定。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you're basically an associate product manager, an IC product manager, an engineer, CPO, COO, CTO, CEO of three different companies including a public company.
zh: 所以你基本上是一个助理产品经理，一个 IC 产品经理，一个工程师，CPO，COO，CTO，三家不同公司的 CEO，包括一家上市公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: Very rare that somebody is successful at all these types of roles and all these levels.
zh: 某人在所有这些类型的角色和所有这些层面上都成功是非常罕见的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, let me just ask you this question.
zh: 那么，让我问你这个问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: What mindsets or habits or just ways of working have you worked on building in yourself that you think have most contributed to you being successful in such a variety of roles and levels?
zh: 你建立了哪些心态、习惯或工作方式，你认为它们最有助于你在如此多种角色和层面上取得成功？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's actually something I am proud of.
zh: 这实际上是我感到自豪的一件事。

speaker: Unknown
en: I like the fact I've worn different hats.
zh: 我喜欢我戴过不同的帽子这一事实。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's actually amusing when I meet colleagues that I've known from one of those jobs, they'll often think of me through the lens of that job.
zh: 当我遇到那些我从其中一份工作中认识的同事时，这其实很有趣，他们通常会通过那份工作的视角来看待我。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I'll go to meet folks from Facebook and they think of me largely as an engineer.
zh: 所以，当我去见 Facebook 的人时，他们主要把我看作一个工程师。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'll meet folks from Google, they think me largely as a product person.
zh: 当我见谷歌的人时，他们主要把我看作一个产品人。

speaker: Unknown
en: At Salesforce, a lot of the folks there interacted with me as like a, lack of a better word, a suit, the boss.
zh: 在 Salesforce，那里很多人与我的互动就像是，没有更好的词了，一个西装革履的人，老板。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I'm not sure they think of me as an engineer at all, even though I was still probably coding on the weekends for fun.
zh: 我不确定他们是否认为我是一个工程师，尽管我可能仍然在周末为了乐趣而写代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: And one of the things that is a principle for me is to have a really flexible view of my own identity.
zh: 对我来说，其中一个原则是对我自己的身份有一个非常灵活的看法。

speaker: Unknown
en: I probably would self-describe as an engineer, but more broadly I think of myself as a builder and I like to build products and I think companies are one of the most effective ways to build products.
zh: 我可能自我描述为一个工程师，但更广泛地说我认为自己是一个建设者，我喜欢构建产品，我认为公司是构建产品的最有效的方式之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's also things like open source, but I think I'm a huge believer in the confluence of technology and capitalism to produce just incredible outcomes for customers.
zh: 还有一些像开源的东西，但我坚信技术和资本的汇合能够为客户带来令人难以置信的成果。

speaker: Unknown
en: And as a consequence, I think to really build something of significance, I think to be a great founder, you really need to be able to not have such a ossified view of your identity that you can't transform into what the company needs you to be at that point.
zh: 因此，我认为要真正构建有意义的东西，要成为一个伟大的创始人，你需要能够不拥有如此僵化的自我观念，以至于你无法转变成为公司在那个时刻需要你成为的样子。

speaker: Unknown
en: And every founder you'll talk to, one day, I think selling is a big part of being a founder.
zh: 你会和每一位创始人交谈，有一天，我认为销售是成为创始人很重要的一部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to sell investors on wanting to invest in your company.
zh: 你必须说服投资者想要投资你的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to sell candidates on wanting to work at your company.
zh: 你必须说服候选人想要为你的公司工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to sell customers to want to use the product that your customer produces.
zh: 你必须说服客户想要使用你客户生产的产品。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to have good design taste, not just for your product but for your marketing and essentially, soliciting your customers.
zh: 你必须有良好的设计品味，不仅是为了你的产品，也是为了你的营销，本质上是为了招揽你的客户。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to have good engineering.
zh: 你必须有良好的工程能力。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you're building a technology company, the technology comes first.
zh: 如果你正在建立一家科技公司，技术是第一位的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's why this industry is so transformative.
zh: 这就是为什么这个行业如此具有变革性。

speaker: Unknown
en: I probably credit, and I've told this story before, but I'm very grateful for her, but I probably credit Sheryl Sandberg for really changing the way I approach new jobs.
zh: 我可能要归功于，我以前讲过这个故事，但我非常感激她，我可能要归功于 Sheryl Sandberg，因为她真的改变了我的方式我接触新工作的方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: The story, and I might be embellishment a little bit, but I think it's broadly accurate.
zh: 这个故事，我可能有点夸张，但我认为它大致是准确的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I had just become the chief technology officer of Facebook and when I first got the job, it was the flavor of CTO or that relatively small group reporting into me, but contributed almost as a very senior architect on a number of projects.
zh: 所以我刚刚成为 Facebook 的首席技术官，当我刚得到这份工作时，它是 CTO 的风格或者是那个相对较小的团队向我汇报，但几乎作为一个非常资深的架构师为许多项目做出贡献。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then at some point, Mark Zuckerberg reorganized the company and split it into a bunch of different groups.
zh: 然后在某个时候，Mark Zuckerberg 重组了公司，把它分成了几个不同的组。

speaker: Unknown
en: I ended up with a very large group, 100 under me and I was essentially running our platform and mobile groups, products, design engineering.
zh: 我最后得到了一个非常大的团队，100 个人向我汇报，我基本上负责我们的平台和移动团队，产品，设计工程。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I went from a handful of reports to, I don't know, over 1,000 or something.
zh: 所以我从手下的几个汇报人变成了，我不知道，超过 1000 人之类的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was a big group.
zh: 那是一个大团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was the largest management job.
zh: 那是最大的管理工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: I had become a manager at Google, but a modest team.
zh: 我在谷歌成为了一名经理，但带的是一个不大的团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I was doing okay but not great.
zh: 所以，我做得还行，但并不出色。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I had this moment where Sheryl saw me, I think I was editing a presentation for a partner just because the presentation I got didn't meet my quality bar and I was editing it and griping about it.
zh: 我有过这样一个时刻，Sheryl 看到了我，我想我当时正在为一个合作伙伴编辑演示文稿，仅仅是因为我拿到的那个演示文稿没有达到我的质量标准，我当时正在编辑它并发牢骚。

speaker: Unknown
en: She pulled me into a room and gave me talking to a little bit about holding my team to as high of a standard as I have.
zh: 她把我拉进一个房间，对我进行了一番谈话，内容是关于让我的团队坚持像我一样高的标准。

speaker: Unknown
en: If someone wasn't meeting my expectations, what was my plan to manage them out of the company or... Just giving me management one-on-one.
zh: 如果有人没有达到我的期望，我有什么计划把他们从公司管理出去或者……只是给我一对一的管理指导。

speaker: Unknown
en: And she's a remarkable mentor in the sense she can give you feedback that's very direct and often, a bit uncomfortable, but you know she cares about you.
zh: 她是一位非凡的导师，在这个意义上，她可以给你非常直接的反馈，而且通常有点让人不舒服，但你知道她关心你。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it was the type of feedback you listen to.
zh: 所以，这是那种你会去听取的反馈。

speaker: Unknown
en: I went home that night and I was stewing on it and not very happy.
zh: 那天晚上我回到家，一直在琢磨这件事，心里很不痛快。

speaker: Unknown
en: I was like, you get naturally a little defensive in those moments.
zh: 你会明白，在那种时刻，人自然会变得有点防御性。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is that really true?
zh: 那是真的吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Am I really fucking it up or is she overreacting?
zh: 我真的搞砸了吗，还是她反应过度了？

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I woke up the next day, I was like, "No, she's right."
zh: 然后第二天我醒来，我想，“不，她是对的。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And I had realized this subconscious limiter that was limiting my success in the job, which is, I was trying to conform the job to the things I thought I liked to do.
zh: 我意识到了那个限制我在工作中取得成功的潜意识限制器，那就是，我试图把工作顺从我自以为我喜欢做的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, I was spending a lot of my time on some product and technology things that I was passionate about, thinking I'm the boss.
zh: 所以，我把大量时间花在我热衷的一些产品和与技术的事情上，想着我是老板。

speaker: Unknown
en: I should focus on what I want to focus on instead of thinking about, okay, I'm running the mobile and platform teams at Facebook.
zh: 我应该专注于我想专注的事情，而不是去思考，好吧，我在负责 Facebook 的移动和平台团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: What's the most important thing to do today to make our mobile and developer platform successful?
zh: 为了让我们的移动和开发者平台取得成功，今天要做的最重要的事情是什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: And when I reframed the job that way, I did different things.
zh: 当我这样重新定义这份工作时，我做了不同的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the thing that was the biggest pleasant surprise to me was I liked it.
zh: 对我来说，最大的意外惊喜是，我喜欢这样。

speaker: Unknown
en: I thought I liked engineering and product, but in fact, when I changed an organization and it turned out to be more successful, I derived a great deal of joy from seeing that success.
zh: 我原以为我喜欢工程和产品，但实际上，当我改变了一个组织并且它变得更成功时，看到那种成功我获得了巨大的快乐。

speaker: Unknown
en: Our developer platform had a lot of partners and when there was an issue there and I'd spend time on partnerships and it worked and our platform became healthier, the partner became more successful.
zh: 我们的开发者平台有很多合作伙伴，当那里出现问题时，我会花时间在合作关系上，而且奏效了，我们的平台变得更健康，合作伙伴也更成功。

speaker: Unknown
en: I took pride in that success and then I just started being better at my job and I realized that the actual act of engineering or product design or all the things I thought I liked, what I really liked is impact.
zh: 我为那种成功感到自豪，然后我开始在工作中做得更好，我意识到，工程或产品设计或所有我原以为我喜欢的事情的实际行为，我真正喜欢的是影响力。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, that conversation led to my waking up every morning, sometimes literally, but certainly, in the broadest sets of the words saying, "What is the most impactful thing I can do today?"
zh: 所以，那次对话导致我每天早上醒来，有时真的是字面意义上的，但当然，在最广泛的意义上说，“我今天能做的最有影响力的事情是什么？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And really thinking almost like, if you had an external board of advisors telling you what are the things where if you focus on them, you can maximize the likelihood that what you're trying to achieve will happen?
zh: 真的几乎是在思考，就像如果你有一个外部顾问委员会告诉你，如果你专注于哪些事情，可以最大化你试图实现的目标发生的可能性？

speaker: Unknown
en: Sometimes, it's recruiting, sometimes, it's product, sometimes, it's engineering, sometimes, it's sales.
zh: 有时，是招聘，有时，是产品，有时，是工程，有时，是销售。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I've become much more self-reflective just about what is important to work on.
zh: 我对什么工作是重要的变得更有自我反省意识了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I have become much more receptive to doing things that I previously would've said aren't my favorite things to do because I derive so much joy from having an impact that I enjoy a lot more things now.
zh: 我也变得更愿意去做那些我以前会说不是我最喜欢做的事情，因为我从产生影响力中获得了如此多的快乐，所以我现在享受更多的事情了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I really credit Sheryl, I'm so grateful.
zh: 所以，我真的要归功于 Sheryl，我非常感激。

speaker: Unknown
en: And actually, it's interesting, I think a lot about this when I give feedback to people now, just those moments that can change the trajectory of your career.
zh: 实际上，这很有趣，我现在给别人反馈时经常想这件事，就是那些能改变你职业轨迹的时刻。

speaker: Unknown
en: I give her all the credit for it.
zh: 我把所有的功劳都归给她。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's so many people that share stories of Sheryl Sandberg giving them advice and that changing their life.
zh: 有很多人分享 Sheryl Sandberg 给他们建议并且改变了他们生活的故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: What a mensch.
zh: 真是个高尚的人。

speaker: Bret Taylor
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: My biggest takeaway from this, which is this question of what is the most impactful thing I could do today?
zh: 我从中最大的收获是这个问题，就是我今天能做的最有影响力的事情是什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: Such a powerful heuristic just to keep in mind.
zh: 这是一个非常强大的启发式方法，只要记在心上就行。

speaker: Unknown
en: To your point, you may realize you don't want to be doing sales or hiring, but if that's the most impactful thing and you end up doing it, you may realize I like this and I'm good at this and have thought about-
zh: 正如你所说的，你可能会意识到你不想做销售或招聘，但如果那是最有影响力的事情，而你最终做了，你可能会意识到我喜欢这个，我擅长这个，并且思考过——

speaker: Unknown
en: Can I double click on that though for a second?
zh: 我能不能在那个问题上再深入一点？

speaker: Unknown
en: Absolutely.
zh: 当然可以。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think it's really hard.
zh: 我觉得这真的很难。

speaker: Unknown
en: One of the dangers for founders and product managers, but I think particularly for founders is incorrect storytelling.
zh: 创始人和产品经理面临的一个危险，但我认为特别是对创始人来说，是错误的叙事。

speaker: Unknown
en: People don't like my product because of X. And if you tell that to yourself and you tell it to your team, all of a sudden, it goes from being an intuition to being a fact.
zh: 人们因为 X 不喜欢我的产品。如果你这样告诉自己，你也告诉你的团队，突然之间，它就从直觉变成了事实。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, you better hope you're right because if you orient your strategy around fixing a problem and you're wrong, your company's going to fail.
zh: 那么，你最好希望你是对的，因为如果你的战略定位是围绕解决问题而你是错的，你的公司就会失败。

speaker: Unknown
en: So why did you lose a deal?
zh: 那么你为什么会失去一笔交易？

speaker: Unknown
en: You could talk to the salesperson who is on the account or perhaps maybe a product manager was involved in the conversation.
zh: 你可以与负责该账户的销售人员谈谈，或者也许可能有产品经理参与了对话。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's very important to have intellectual honesty in those moments because you could say something like, "Oh, they didn't buy it because the platform cost too much."
zh: 在那些时刻拥有智识上的诚实非常重要，因为你可以这样说，“噢，他们没买是因为平台成本太高了。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's something a salesperson might say.
zh: 这是销售人员可能会说的话。

speaker: Unknown
en: Maybe the real reason is they didn't actually see much value in your platform.
zh: 也许真正的原因是他们实际上没有在你的平台上看到太大的价值。

speaker: Unknown
en: So it was communicated to the salesperson as it was too expensive.
zh: 所以传达给销售人员的信息是它太贵了。

speaker: Unknown
en: But in fact, the problem was product differentiation.
zh: 但实际上，问题是产品差异化。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you could end up going into a discussion on pricing when in fact, there was a much deeper, much harder problem to solve there.
zh: 你最终可能会进入关于定价的讨论，但实际上，那里有一个更深、更难解决的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: But just like when you break up with someone, you don't say, it's because I don't like you anymore.
zh: 但就像当你和某人分手时，你不会说，是因为我不再喜欢你了。

speaker: Unknown
en: You say it's not you, it's me.
zh: 你会说，不是你的问题，是我的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: You say all these pleasantries because we're all social animals and you want to be pleasant with the people around you.
zh: 你说所有这些客套话，因为我们都是社会性动物，你想让你身边的人感到愉快。

speaker: Unknown
en: So literally taking what a customer says or what a user says in a focus group or a usability study is rarely correct.
zh: 所以，字面上采用客户在焦点小组或可用性研究中说的话，或者用户说的话，很少是正确的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It often is related to what the truth is, but it's very important to get right.
zh: 它通常与真相相关，但这非常重要的是要弄对。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I think one of the things I've observed with first time founders in particular is you're often a single issue voter based on your skillset.
zh: 所以，我认为我观察到的一件事，尤其是对于首次创业者，是你往往是基于你的技能集的单一议题投票者。

speaker: Unknown
en: So if you're a great engineer, the answer to almost every problem in your business is engineering.
zh: 所以如果你是一个伟大的工程师，你业务中几乎每个问题的答案都是工程。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you're a product designer, the answer almost to the proverbial redesign, I joke, it's like the dead cap balance of a consumer product like this next redesign will fix all of our problems.
zh: 如果你是一个产品设计师，答案几乎都是谚语般的重新设计，我开玩笑说，这就像消费品的死帽余额，像这下一次重新设计将解决我们所有的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't know if it's ever, ever worked.
zh: 我不知道它是否曾经，曾经有效过。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I met a lot of entrepreneurs who come from a business development background, they're always thinking about partnerships and oh, if we just get this partnership done for this distribution channel, everything's going to change.
zh: 然后我遇到了很多来自业务发展背景的企业家，他们总是在考虑合作关系，哦，如果我们只要为这个分销渠道完成这个合作关系，一切都会改变。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think it's really important when you're a founder to be self-aware that you will naturally, subconsciously pick the thing that is your strength, your superpower as a solution to more problems.
zh: 我认为当你作为创始人时，非常重要的是要有自我意识，你会自然地、下意识地选择那个作为你的优势、你的超能力的事物，作为更多问题的解决方案。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in fact, if you think that's a solution to your problem, it may be right, but you probably by default should question it.
zh: 实际上，如果你认为那是对你问题的解决方案，它可能是对的，但你可能默认应该质疑它。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you think the thing that you've been doing your whole career is the way to fix your problem, it's at least 30% likely that you've chosen that because of comfort and familiarity not truth.
zh: 如果你认为你整个职业生涯一直在做的事情是解决问题的方法，那么至少有 30% 的可能性你选择它是因为舒适和熟悉，而不是真相。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I think one of the skills I think is, it really goes around to do you have a good co-founder?
zh: 所以，我认为其中一项技能我认为是，它真的归结为你是否有一个好的联合创始人？

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you have a good leadership team?
zh: 你是否有一个好的领导团队？

speaker: Unknown
en: If you're a product manager, you're a partner in engineering, you're a partner in marketing, you really want to have very real conversations to ensure that you're actually working on the actual correct thing.
zh: 如果你是一个产品经理，你是工程领域的合作伙伴，你是营销领域的合作伙伴，你真的想要进行非常真实的对话，以确保你实际上正在处理实际正确的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think it's easy to say what's the most impactful thing to do today?
zh: 我认为很容易说今天做什么是最有影响力的？

speaker: Unknown
en: My guess, if a lot of people try that, they'll lie to themselves more often than not.
zh: 我的猜测是，如果很多人尝试这样做，他们往往会对自已撒谎。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's a very challenging question to answer.
zh: 这是一个非常具有挑战性的问题去回答。

speaker: Unknown
en: The question's interesting.
zh: 这个问题很有趣。

speaker: Unknown
en: Being able to answer it accurately is actually the hard part.
zh: 能够准确地回答它实际上才是困难的部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: This feels like such an important lesson you've learned.
zh: 这感觉像是你学到的一个如此重要的教训。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is there an example that comes to mind where you learned this the hard way where you actually ended up-
zh: 有没有想到一个例子，你是通过艰难的方式学到这一点的，你实际上最终——

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh, yeah.
zh: 哦，是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: You just want to spend this whole thing on my failures, but I'm fine with that.
zh: 你只是想把这整个事情都花在我的失败上，但我对此没问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: You've had too much success.
zh: 你有过太多的成功。

speaker: Unknown
en: Frontier was my first company.
zh: Frontier 是我的第一家公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: At our peak we had 12 employees, 12 of the best people I've ever worked with.
zh: 在我们的巅峰时期，我们有 12 名员工，他们是我共事过的最好的 12 个人。

speaker: Unknown
en: Started the company with Jim Norris, who's an engineer I've known since Stanford and Paul Buhite and Sanjeev Singh who Paul started Gmail.
zh: 我和 Jim Norris 一起创办了公司，Jim Norris 是我自斯坦福以来就认识的一位工程师，还有 Paul Buhite 和 Sanjeev Singh，Paul 创立了 Gmail。

speaker: Unknown
en: Sanjeev was the first engineer at Gmail, so we had the Google Maps people and Gmail people.
zh: Sanjeev 是 Gmail 的第一位工程师，所以我们有 Google Maps 的人和 Gmail 的人。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was a pretty awesome founding team.
zh: 这是一个非常棒的创始团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: We made a social network, as you said.
zh: 我们做了一个社交网络，正如你所说的。

speaker: Unknown
en: We invented a lot of concepts that became popular in the newsfeed.
zh: 我们发明了许多在新闻源中变得流行的概念。

speaker: Unknown
en: We invented the like button.
zh: 我们发明了点赞按钮。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was really neat.
zh: 这真的很棒。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was a fun time.
zh: 那是一段有趣的时光。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were only really popular in Turkey, Italy and Iran, and at one point, we were blocked in Iran, so we were only popular in Turkey and Italy and Silicon Valley.
zh: 我们实际上只在土耳其、意大利和伊朗很受欢迎，在某一时刻，我们在伊朗被封锁了，所以我们只在土耳其和意大利以及硅谷很受欢迎。

speaker: Unknown
en: To this day, actually a lot of folks in Silicon Valley are like, "I love FriendFeed."
zh: 直到今天，实际上硅谷的很多人都说，“我爱 FriendFeed。”

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm like, that's awesome.
zh: 我会说，那太棒了。

speaker: Unknown
en: It wasn't really a successful business.
zh: 它实际上不是一个成功的生意。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were a follower-oriented social network, not a friendship-oriented social network, which meant a lot of our content was more like X or Twitter than it is Facebook in that respect.
zh: 我们是一个关注者导向的社交网络，而不是友谊导向的社交网络，这意味着我们的很多内容更像 X 或 Twitter，而不是 Facebook 在这方面。

speaker: Unknown
en: And a lot of sharing newspaper articles, interests, scientific communities, things like that.
zh: 并且有很多分享报纸文章、兴趣、科学社区之类的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there was a period when Twitter, which was one of our competitors at the time, that there was a lot more social networks at the time.
zh: 有一个时期，Twitter，当时是我们竞争对手之一，当时有更多的社交网络。

speaker: Unknown
en: I am probably screwing this up a little bit.
zh: 我可能把这一点搞砸了一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think Obama, Ashton Kutcher and Oprah Winfrey all went on Twitter in a summer and we just got our ass kicked.
zh: 我认为奥巴马、阿什顿·库彻和奥普拉·温弗瑞都在那个夏天加入了 Twitter，我们就这样被踢了屁股。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was a great example of you... I think 11 of those 12 people were engineers and we were just making product and I think it was Biz Stone.
zh: 这是一个很好的例子……我认为那 12 个人中有 11 个是工程师，我们只是在制造产品，我认为是 Biz Stone。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you talk to the Twitter folks, they could give you the history on this, but I think Biz was really focused on getting celebrities and public figures onto Twitter, which is totally obvious.
zh: 如果你和 Twitter 的人交谈，他们可以给你这段历史，但我认为 Biz 真的专注于让名人和公众人物加入 Twitter，这完全是显而易见的。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you have a social service that's oriented towards following people, put some people on there worth following and instead, we were exclusively focused on polishing the product.
zh: 如果你有一个专注于关注人的社交服务，在上面放一些值得关注的人，而我们却完全专注于打磨产品。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we actually, I think at our peak of popularity, we were very confident just, I think it was a time when Twitter had the fail whale and it was down half the time and people couldn't even use it.
zh: 实际上，我认为在我们最受欢迎的巅峰时期，我们非常自信，只是，我认为那是 Twitter 有故障鲸鱼的时候，它有一半时间都在宕机，人们甚至无法使用它。

speaker: Unknown
en: And our product, we were innovating faster, we had more features, people liked it and we were up 100% of the time and we totally lost for no reason related to product at all.
zh: 我们的产品，我们创新得更快，我们有更多功能，人们喜欢它，而且我们 100% 的时间都在线，结果我们完全输了，原因与产品毫无关系。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was an example of, I think somewhat famously not a lot of great entrepreneurs have come out of Google because Google was so successful, I think it's hard as a product manager to see distribution and product design and even business model when you have AdWords and money's raining from the sky.
zh: 这是一个例子，我认为某种程度上出了名的，没有多少伟大的企业家从 Google 走出来，因为 Google 太成功了，我认为作为一个产品经理，当你有 AdWords 且钱从天上掉下来时，很难看清分发、产品设计甚至商业模式。

speaker: Unknown
en: There wasn't as much scrutiny and I think folks like the PayPal Mafia I think learned a lot more about entrepreneurialism than a typical PM at Google.
zh: 那里没有那么多审查，我认为像 PayPal 黑帮这样的人，我认为他们比 Google 的典型 PM 学到了更多关于企业家精神的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, we're just getting punched in the face and learning this the hard way.
zh: 所以，我们只是被迎头痛击，艰难地吸取了教训。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, that was probably the most prominent example of it and I think we probably did have a... I can tell you all the flaws of that product, but I don't think that was the reason why we lost.
zh: 所以，那可能是最突出的例子，我认为我们确实有一个……我可以告诉你那个产品的所有缺陷，但我不认为那是我们输掉的原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's a lot of reasons.
zh: 原因有很多。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think there was a lot of flaws of the product, but it was a lot of other stuff.
zh: 我认为产品有很多缺陷，但还有其他很多因素。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I've learned, accumulated these skills over time, but I say the hard part of that question is answering it correctly, is it's hard when you don't have experience in something, than to have intuition in it.
zh: 所以，我学到了，随着时间的推移积累了这些技能，但我说这个问题最难的部分是正确回答它，当你对某事没有经验时，很难对它有直觉。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think if there's probably a structural flaw, it wasn't that... I don't know if I could have figured out how to reach out to Ashton Kutcher [inaudible 00:27:28], it's not he's on my Rolodex.
zh: 所以我认为如果可能有一个结构性的缺陷，那并不是……我不知道我是否能弄清楚如何联系 Ashton Kutcher [听不清 00:27:28]，他不在我的名片盒里。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I probably wasn't soliciting advice from the right people.
zh: 但我可能没有向合适的人寻求建议。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think that what's great about the technology industry is there's a lot of advice.
zh: 我认为科技行业好的一点是有很多建议。

speaker: Unknown
en: Choosing whom you listen to is actually quite difficult, but I think we're somewhat myopic.
zh: 选择听谁的话实际上相当困难，但我认为我们有些目光短浅。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're in our own little world, creating this product and we weren't asking people from the outside in to say, what are you seeing that could go wrong?
zh: 我们在我们自己的小世界里，创造这个产品，我们没有从外面请人进来说，你看到什么可能会出错？

speaker: Unknown
en: What are you seeing that could go right?
zh: 你看到什么可能会做对？

speaker: Unknown
en: What are you seeing in the industry that we're not doing that you think we might want to do?
zh: 你看到我们在行业里没做的事情是你觉得我们可能想要做的？

speaker: Unknown
en: And this is why boards are important.
zh: 这就是为什么董事会很重要。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is why finding the right advisors, the advisors will actually tell you what you not [inaudible 00:28:09] want to hear, but you need to hear.
zh: 这就是为什么找到合适的顾问很重要，这些顾问实际上会告诉你你不想 [听不清 00:28:09] 听到，但你需要听到的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think that was probably the missing part.
zh: 我认为那可能是缺失的部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm not sure I was great at market at the time, but if I had solicited the right advice, I could have learned that that was a shortcoming.
zh: 我不确定我当时是否擅长市场，但如果我寻求了正确的建议，我可能已经学到那是一个短板。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think that was a deep lesson I took from that.
zh: 我认为那是我从中学到的深刻教训。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm a huge believer in boards and getting good advice.
zh: 我非常相信董事会和获得好的建议。

speaker: Unknown
en: Any heuristics or advice for people to know whose advice to listen to?
zh: 对于人们要知道听谁的建议，有什么启发式或建议吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: What do you pay attention to when you're like, okay, ignore this person but listen to this person?
zh: 当你就像，好吧，忽略这个人但听这个人的时候，你关注什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, that one's tough.
zh: 是的，那个很难。

speaker: Unknown
en: It does come down to good judgment and being judge of people's character.
zh: 这确实归结为良好的判断力和作为评判人的性格的能力。

speaker: Unknown
en: One thing that is particularly hard is there's not a strong correlation between the confidence with which someone expresses an opinion and the quality of that opinion.
zh: 特别难的一点是，一个人表达观点的自信程度与该观点的质量之间没有很强的相关性。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't want to say it's inversely correlated, but that's funny, with all the podcasts out now, if there's topics I know a lot about, sometimes the most eloquent, confident statements about things I know a lot about, are the least accurate and it sounds extremely persuasive.
zh: 我不想说它是负相关的，但这很有趣，随着现在所有播客的出现，如果有一些我了解很多的主题，有时关于我了解很多的主题的最雄辩、最自信的陈述，是最不准确的，而且听起来非常有说服力。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, it does require very good judgment.
zh: 所以，这确实需要非常好的判断力。

speaker: Unknown
en: One thing is I think, not just asking for advice but asking people, who should I talk to get good advice?
zh: 一件事是，我认为，不仅仅是寻求建议，而是问人们，我应该和谁交谈以获得好的建议？

speaker: Unknown
en: And you'll find some common answers there and that's often a really strong signal of good judgment.
zh: 你会在那里发现一些共同的答案，这通常是良好判断力的一个非常强烈的信号。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then one thing I found is when you ask for advice, don't just ask what to do but why.
zh: 然后我发现的一件事是，当你寻求建议时，不要只问做什么，还要问为什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: Be an obnoxious two-year-old kid, why?
zh: 做一个讨厌的两岁小孩，为什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: Why?
zh: 为什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: Why?
zh: 为什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: Why?
zh: 为什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: And really try to understand the framework that someone is using to give you advice.
zh: 并真正试着理解某人用来给你建议的框架。

speaker: Unknown
en: The interesting thing about advice is people are often extrapolating from relatively few experiences.
zh: 关于建议的一个有趣点是，人们经常从相对较少的经验中进行推断。

speaker: Unknown
en: So they will say, never do this or always do that.
zh: 所以他们会说，永远不要做这个或总是做那个。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's because they had one experience where something backfired or something could have gone better if they had done it.
zh: 这是因为他们有过一次经历，某事产生了反效果，或者如果他们做了某事可能会更好。

speaker: Unknown
en: So it's a useful anecdote, but if you don't ask why and understand they had one experience and here's what happened, it can come across as a rule when in fact, it's [inaudible 00:30:08] data and if you ask advice of three people and they all have very similar interactions, you can create a first principles framework from which that advice emerges.
zh: 所以这是一个有用的轶事，但如果你不问为什么并理解他们有过一次经历并且这里是发生的事情，它可能会作为一个规则出现，事实上，它是 [听不清 00:30:08] 数据，如果你询问三个人的建议并且他们都有非常相似的互动，你可以创建一个第一性原理框架，建议从中产生。

speaker: Unknown
en: And when you start applying it, you're applying it with a degree of nuance that you couldn't if you're just following a rule.
zh: 当你开始应用它时，你是带着一定程度的应用它，如果你只是遵循规则就无法做到这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, I think one is, it does come down to good judgment, I think.
zh: 所以，我认为一个是，我认为这确实归结为良好的判断力。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't know how to teach that.
zh: 我不知道如何教授那个。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm a huge believer in good judgment.
zh: 我非常相信良好的判断力。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's one of the things I hire for.
zh: 这是我招聘的要素之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: I just think that's something that probably comes from a mix of self perfection.
zh: 我只是认为这可能来自自我完善的混合体。

speaker: Unknown
en: You really need to hold yourselves accountable as an entrepreneur, as a product manager.
zh: 你真的需要作为一个企业家，作为一个产品经理，对自己负责。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you made a bad decision, spend time reflecting on it, number one.
zh: 如果你做了一个错误的决定，花时间反思它，第一。

speaker: Unknown
en: And really, try to understand why and try to always improve your judgment.
zh: 并且真的，试着理解为什么，并试着总是提高你的判断力。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think at the end of the day, that is why you are a good entrepreneur, a good product manager.
zh: 我认为归根结底，这就是你之所以成为好的企业家、好的产品经理的原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: And number two, when you get advice, really understand where it's coming from and why so that you can create your own independent view of where that advice came from and recognize that no one's advice is statistically significant or very rarely is it.
zh: 第二点,当你得到建议时,真正理解它的来源和原因,这样你就能对那个建议的来源形成自己独立的看法,并认识到没有任何人的建议具有统计显著性,或者很少有建议是具有统计显著性的。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you're getting advice on investing from Warren Buffett, yeah, okay, it's statistically significant, but most advice is like something happened to you once and you have regrets.
zh: 如果你从沃伦·巴菲特那里获得投资建议,是的,好吧,那具有统计显著性,但大多数建议就像是某件事在你身上发生过一次,而你有遗憾。

speaker: Unknown
en: I love that you're like, I don't know if I have a great answer then you just give us an incredible answer to this question.
zh: 我喜欢你刚才那样说,我不知道我是否有很好的答案,然后你就给了我们这个问题的一个令人难以置信的答案。

speaker: Unknown
en: I want to go in a different direction.
zh: 我想换个方向。

speaker: Unknown
en: You mentioned that you describe yourself as an engineer.
zh: 你提到你把自己描述为一个工程师。

speaker: Unknown
en: I know I heard you code to relax still.
zh: 我知道我听说你为了放松仍然在写代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: Let me just ask you this question, something a lot of people in college are thinking about.
zh: 就让我问你这个问题,很多大学生都在思考的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you think it still makes sense to learn to code?
zh: 你认为学习编程还有意义吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you think this will significantly change in the next few years?
zh: 你认为这在未来几年会发生重大变化吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: I do still think studying computer science is a different answer than learning to code, but I would say I still think it's extremely valuable to study computer science.
zh: 我确实仍然认为学习计算机科学和学习编程是不同的答案,但我会说我仍然认为学习计算机科学是非常有价值的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I say that because I think computer science is more than coding.
zh: 我这么说是因为我认为计算机科学不仅仅是编程。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you understand things like Big O notation or complexity theory or study algorithms and why a randomized algorithm works and why two algorithms with the same Big O complexity, one can then practice perform better than others and why a cache miss matters and just all these little... There's a lot more to coding than writing the code.
zh: 如果你理解像大 O 表示法或复杂性理论之类的东西,或者研究算法以及为什么随机算法有效,以及为什么两个具有相同大 O 复杂度的算法,其中一个在实践中可能比另一个表现更好,以及为什么缓存命中很重要,以及所有这些小细节……编程不仅仅是编写代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: The reason I think that is I do think the act of creating software is going to transform from typing into a terminal or typing into Visual Studio code to operating a code-generating machine.
zh: 我认为这样的原因是,我确实认为创建软件的行为将从输入到终端或输入到 Visual Studio 代码转变为操作一台代码生成机器。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think that is the future of creating software.
zh: 我认为这就是创建软件的未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I think operating a code-generating machine requires systems thinking and I think that computer science, there are other disciplines as well, but computer science is a wonderful major to learn systems thinking and at the end of the day, AI will facilitate creating this software.
zh: 但我认为操作一台代码生成机器需要系统思维,我认为计算机科学,还有其他学科,但计算机科学是学习系统思维的一个很好的专业,归根结底,人工智能将有助于创建这种软件。

speaker: Unknown
en: We may do a lot more in the next few years we can't even imagine, but your job as the operator of that code-generating machine is to make a product or to solve a problem and you really need to have great systems thinking and you're going to be managing this machine that's doing a lot of the tedious work of making the button or connecting to the network.
zh: 我们在未来几年可能会做很多我们甚至无法想象的事情,但你作为那台代码生成机器的操作员,你的工作是制造产品或解决问题,你真的需要具备很好的系统思维,你将管理这台正在做很多琐碎工作的机器,比如制作按钮或连接网络。

speaker: Unknown
en: But as you're thinking of the intersection of a technology and a business problem, you're trying to affect a system that will solve that problem at scale for your customers and that systems thinking is always the hardest part of creating products.
zh: 但是当你思考技术和商业问题的交集时,你正在尝试设计一个能够大规模为你的客户解决该问题的系统,而这种系统思维总是创建产品中最难的部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'll just give you, it's this cheesy simple example, but I think it's representative.
zh: 我就给你举个例子,这是一个有点俗套的简单例子,但我认为它具有代表性。

speaker: Unknown
en: At Facebook, we spent a lot of time designing the newsfeed and if you ever had a really, really good designer and they showed you at the time, a Photoshop mock-up of the newsfeed, it was just all as beautiful.
zh: 在 Facebook,我们花了很多时间设计信息流,如果你曾经有一个非常好的设计师,他们在那个时候向你展示了信息流的 Photoshop 模型,它一切都是美丽的。

speaker: Unknown
en: The photos, the family was happy and the photo was a perfect photo and the posts were all perfectly grammatically correct and of a completely normal length and the comments and there was the like... Everything was just perfect.
zh: 照片,家庭是幸福的,照片是一张完美的照片,帖子在语法上都是完全正确的,长度也是完全正常的,还有评论,还有那个点赞……一切都是完美的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then you'd implement that design and you'd look at your own newsfeed and it looked like shit because it turns out not everyone's photos were made by a professional photographer.
zh: 然后你实现了那个设计,你看着你自己的信息流,它看起来像垃圾,因为事实证明并非所有人的照片都是由专业摄影师制作的。

speaker: Unknown
en: The posts were all these different lengths.
zh: 帖子的长度都各不相同。

speaker: Unknown
en: The comments were like, you suck and... All that stuff.
zh: 评论就像是,你真烂等等。所有的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then all of a sudden you realize that designing a newsfeed, Photoshop is the easy part.
zh: 然后突然之间你意识到设计一个信息流,Photoshop 部分是容易的部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: You need to actually design a system that produces both in content and visual design, like a delightful experience given input you don't control.
zh: 你需要实际设计一个能够在内容内容和视觉设计上产生愉悦体验的系统,给定你无法控制的输入。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's a system, it's sort of a design and it's just, what we did practically, I am sure it's changed a lot since I left in 2012, but we made a system so designers had to show their newsfeed designs with real newsfeed data that was messy rather than anything artificial because I think it forced the process to be more realistic.
zh: 而且那是一个系统,它是一种设计,实际上我们所做的,我确信自从 2012 年我离开以来它已经发生了很多变化,但我们做了一个系统,所以设计师必须用真实的信息流数据展示他们的信息流设计,那是杂乱的,而不是任何人工的东西,因为我认为它迫使这个过程更加现实。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I say that because I think that whether AI is writing code or doing the design or doing all these other things, you need to learn how to have a system in your head.
zh: 但我这么说是因为我认为,无论是人工智能在编写代码还是在做设计还是在做所有其他事情,你需要学习如何在你的脑海中建立一个系统。

speaker: Unknown
en: You need to understand the basics of what's hard and what's easy and what's possible and what's impossible.
zh: 你需要理解什么是难的,什么是容易的,什么是可能的,什么是不可能的的基本原理。

speaker: Unknown
en: And AI can help you do that too, by the way.
zh: 顺便说一下,人工智能也可以帮助你做到这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I do think that's a really useful skill.
zh: 但我确实那是一个非常有用的技能。 [[330 我认为总的来说,随着人工智能智能体的出现和人工智能在特定领域接近超级智能,我认为我们用以完成工作的工具将发生很大变化。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think in general, with the advent of AI agents and AI approaching super intelligence in certain domains, I think the tools with which we do our job will change a lot.
zh: 我认为总体而言，随着 AI 智能体的出现以及 AI 在某些领域接近超级智能，我认为我们要用来完成工作的工具将会发生很大变化。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think it's very important to have a very loose attachment to the way we do our jobs and that story that we won't talk about when I rewrote Google Maps, everyone talks about that story and I think it's because of Paul [inaudible 00:35:57] who told it on some podcasts and that's where it made the rounds.
zh: 我认为对我们完成工作的方式保持一种非常宽松的依附关系是非常重要的,那个我们不谈论的故事,当我重写 Google Maps 时,每个人都在谈论那个故事,我认为这是因为 Paul [听不清 00:35:57] 在一些播客上讲述了它,那就是它流传开来的原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think that's going to end up this vestige of the past, almost like the human calculators at NASA before the computers were invented, like wow, a person was a calculator?
zh: 我认为那最终将成为过去的遗迹,就像计算机发明之前 NASA 的人工计算员一样,哇,一个人是一台计算器?

speaker: Unknown
en: Whoa, that's fun.
zh: 哇,那真有趣。

speaker: Unknown
en: Tell me that story.
zh: 给我讲讲那个故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think just what I was good at will no longer be useful in the future or certainly not valuable in the future and that's okay.
zh: 我认为只是我擅长的东西在未来将不再有用,或者在未来肯定没有价值,但这没关系。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think we need to have a really loose view of it, but the idea that you shouldn't study these disciplines, it's like people say, I don't want to study math because I'm not going to use it in my career for X. Well, studying maths is quite important.
zh: 所以我认为我们需要对此有一个非常宽松的看法,但是你不应该学习这些学科的想法,就像人们说,我不想学习数学,因为我在我的职业生涯中不会使用它来做 X。好吧,学习数学是很重要的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It teaches you how to think.
zh: 它教会你如何思考。

speaker: Unknown
en: It teaches you how the world works, physics, math, and I think computer science especially, at least the foundations of it, will continue to be the foundations of how we build software and understanding that when you're interacting particularly with something that's smarter than you, producing code you might not completely understand how you constrain it and how you get it to produce these outcomes.
zh: 它教会你世界是如何运作的,物理,数学,我认为计算机科学尤其如此,至少是其基础,将继续成为我们如何构建软件的基础,并且理解这一点,当你与某种比你更聪明的东西互动时,产生你可能不完全理解的代码,你如何约束它以及你如何让它产生这些结果。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think it will require a lot of sophistication actually.
zh: 我认为这实际上需要很多 sophistication(复杂性/老练/精细度)。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's such a great answer.
zh: 这是一个很好的答案。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's this always sense of this binary, should I learn to code or not?
zh: 总是有这种二元对立的感觉,我应该学习编程还是不学习?

speaker: Unknown
en: And your point here is learn to understand how engineering works and how systems work and what your code does and how it all interconnects, but the way you actually do the coding at your desk will change significantly.
zh: 你的观点是,学习理解工程是如何工作的,系统是如何工作的,你的代码做什么,以及它们是如何相互连接的,但是你在办公桌前实际进行编程的方式将发生重大变化。

speaker: Unknown
en: This reminds me of something you mentioned on a podcast recently.
zh: 这让我想起了你最近在播客上提到的一些事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: This idea that you think there's going to, or there should be a new programming language that is more designed for LLMs versus humans.
zh: 你认为会出现,或者应该出现一种新的编程语言,它更多的是为 LLM 设计而不是为人类设计的想法。

speaker: Unknown
en: Can you just talk about that because I think a lot of people aren't thinking about that?
zh: 你能谈谈这个吗,因为我认为很多人没有考虑到这一点?

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't know if it's a language, I would call it a programming system because I think language might be too limited.
zh: 我不知道它是不是一种语言,我会称之为一个编程系统,因为我认为语言可能太局限了。

speaker: Unknown
en: My reductive version of the past, what 40 years of computers maybe more, is we created the hardware for computers, then we created punch cards, which is the way in the late '70s you would tell a computer what to do or maybe mid to late '70s.
zh: 我对过去的简化版本,大概 40 年的计算机历史也许更多,是我们为计算机创建了硬件,然后我们创建了穿孔卡片,这是在 70 年代末你告诉计算机做什么的方式,或者是 70 年代中后期。

speaker: Unknown
en: Then we invented early operating systems and time-sharing systems from the invention of things like Unix at Bell Labs and Berkeley, you ended up with the C programming language, Fortran and a lot of higher level programming languages.
zh: 然后我们发明了早期的操作系统和分时系统,从贝尔实验室和伯克利发明 Unix 这样的事情开始,你最终得到了 C 编程语言,Fortran 和许多更高级别的编程语言。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think Fortran and then C.
zh: 我认为 Fortran 然后是 C。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we moved up the layers of abstraction.
zh: 而我们向上移动了抽象层的层级。

speaker: Unknown
en: No one does punch cards anymore, obviously.
zh: 很明显,再也没有人使用打孔卡了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Few people write assembly language.
zh: 很少有人编写汇编语言。

speaker: Unknown
en: Some people write C, some people write REST.
zh: 有些人写 C,有些人写 REST。

speaker: Unknown
en: But a lot of people write Python and TypeScript and things like that.
zh: 但很多人编写 Python 和 TypeScript 以及类似的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And as we've invented more and more abstractions, we've made it easier to do high-leverage things.
zh: 随着我们发明了越来越多的抽象,我们使得做高杠杆作用的事情变得更容易。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, if you look at how remarkable Google was back in the day or Google Maps, you could probably give a lot of react programmers the task of make a draggable map now and I think a lot of people could do it.
zh: 所以,如果你看看当年的 Google 有多么非凡,或者 Google 地图,你现在大概可以给很多 react 程序员分配制作一个可拖动地图的任务,我认为很多人都能做到。

speaker: Unknown
en: That was true RND back in the day.
zh: 那在当年是真正的研发。

speaker: Unknown
en: When Salesforce was created in 1998, just putting a database in the cloud was hard and that alone was a technical moat that is now trivial with Amazon Web Services and that technical moat is comically narrow, but the product moat is quite large.
zh: 当 Salesforce 在 1998 年被创建时,仅仅把一个数据库放到云端就是困难的,那本身就是一个技术护城河,而现在这在 Amazon Web Services 上是微不足道的,那个技术护城河现在可笑地狭窄,但产品护城河是相当大的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think that if the act of writing code is going from something that is very costly to the marginal cost of that going to zero, how many of the abstractions that we've built are based on human program or productivity?
zh: 我认为,如果编写代码的行为正在从非常昂贵的事情转变为其边际成本趋近于零,那么我们构建的抽象中有多少是基于人类程序员或生产力的?

speaker: Unknown
en: I think a ton.
zh: 我想有很多。

speaker: Unknown
en: I always laugh that I assume Python is probably the most common generated code just because of how much it's in the training data and data scientists love Python and I love Python too.
zh: 我总是笑着假设,Python 可能是最常见的生成代码,只是因为它是训练数据中出现得多么频繁,而且数据科学家喜欢 Python,我也喜欢 Python。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's such a comically bad thing for AI to generate just because it's one of the most inefficient programming languages of all time.
zh: 对于 AI 来说,生成这东西是一个可笑的糟糕选择,因为它是史上效率最低的编程语言之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you know the global interpreter lock and just slow.
zh: 如果你知道全局解释器锁,并且它就是慢。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I've written a lot of high-scale web services and it's just quite slow and it's very hard to verify.
zh: 我写过很多高规模的 Web 服务,它就是很慢,而且很难验证。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's not as bad as Perl, but if you have a big Python program, how many errors will you find at runtime versus before releasing it?
zh: 它没有 Perl 那么糟,但是如果你有一个大型的 Python 程序,你会发现在运行时有多少错误,而不是在发布它之前?

speaker: Unknown
en: So, Python was designed to be very ergonomic, almost looked like pseudo code for humans, for me to write code in a delightful way.
zh: 所以,Python 被设计得非常符合人体工程学,几乎看起来像是给人看的伪代码,为了让我以令人愉悦的方式编写代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's why data scientists love it so much.
zh: 这就是数据科学家如此喜欢它的原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: So as we move to a world where let's just postulate, and I'm not sure this will be completely true, that we're not going to write a lot of code as people.
zh: 所以,当我们进入一个这样的世界时,让我们先假设一下,我不确定这是否会完全成真,我们人类将不再编写大量代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're going to be operating these code-generating machines.
zh: 我们将操作这些代码生成机器。

speaker: Unknown
en: We probably don't care how ergonomic the programming language is.
zh: 我们可能不再关心编程语言的人体工程学如何。

speaker: Unknown
en: What we care about is when this machine generates code, do we know that it did what we wanted it to do?
zh: 我们关心的是当这台机器生成代码时,我们是否知道它做了我们想让它做的事?

speaker: Unknown
en: And if it doesn't do we want it to do, can we change it easily?
zh: 如果它没做我们想让它做的事,我们能轻松地改变它吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: I think there's a lot of insights in programming languages that could serve this.
zh: 我认为编程语言中有很多见解可以为这个目的服务。

speaker: Unknown
en: So Rust I think, is interesting because if I asked you to look at a C program and say, "Does it leak memory?"
zh: 所以 Rust 我认为很有趣,因为如果我让你看一个 C 程序并说,"它会泄漏内存吗?"

speaker: Unknown
en: You probably couldn't do it that well just because it's really hard and if it's a very, a million line C program, it's going to be very, very hard.
zh: 你大概做得不是很好,因为这真的很难,而且如果那是一个一百万行的 C 程序,那将是非常、非常困难的。

speaker: Unknown
en: If I asked you to verify that a Rust program doesn't leak memory, you would just have to compile it.
zh: 如果我让你验证一个 Rust 程序不会泄漏内存,你只需要编译它。

speaker: Unknown
en: And because it has compile time, memory safety, just the act of compiling successfully tells you that's true.
zh: 因为它具有编译时内存安全性,仅仅编译成功这一行为就告诉你那是真的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think we need more things like that because if an AI is generating this code, by definition, if you have to read every line that is going to be the limiting factor for producing the code or worse, you're just not going to read every line and you're going to emit a bunch of unsafe unverified code into the wild.
zh: 我认为我们需要更多类似的东西,因为如果 AI 正在生成这些代码,根据定义,如果你必须阅读每一行,那将是生产代码的制约因素,或者更糟的是,你只是不会阅读每一行,而且你将向世界发布一堆不安全、未经验证的代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, the question is how do you enable humans to have as much leverage as possible?
zh: 所以,问题是如何让人类拥有尽可能大的杠杆作用?

speaker: Unknown
en: Which means using computers to do the work on your behalf.
zh: 这意味着使用计算机代表你去做工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: You could have obviously the simplest form of this, is AI supervising AI and doing code reviews and that's great.
zh: 你显然可以有最简单的形式,就是 AI 监督 AI 并进行代码审查,这很棒。

speaker: Unknown
en: Certainly, self-reflection is a really effective way of improving the robustness of an AI system.
zh: 当然,自我反思是提高 AI 系统鲁棒性的一种非常有效的方法。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I do think if it doesn't matter how tedious it is to write the code, you could probably layer on some techniques that are out of fashion, like formal verification, unit testing, other things.
zh: 但我确实认为,如果编写代码有多繁琐并不重要,你可能会叠加一些过时的技术,比如形式化验证,单元测试,以及其他东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And if you layer all these on, I'm thinking about it as, I as a... It's like the guy in the matrix with the green letters coming down, how can I make something so I as a operator of the code generating machine can produce incredibly complex scale software, incredibly quickly and know that it works?
zh: 如果你把所有这些都叠加起来,我在思考这就像,我作为一个……这就像《黑客帝国》里那个有绿色字母落下来的人,我怎样才能制造某种东西,以便我作为代码生成机器的操作员,能够以令人难以置信的速度生产极其复杂的大规模软件,并且知道它是有效的?

speaker: Unknown
en: If you start with that as your design center, I think you'd probably changed the languages, you'd probably changed the systems, you'd probably change all these things and you're probably going to bring to bear a lot of things.
zh: 如果你以此作为你的设计中心,我认为你可能会改变语言,你可能会改变系统,你可能会改变所有这些东西,并且你可能会引入很多东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what's really fun about it is you can loosen a lot of constraints, like coding is free.
zh: 真正有趣的是,你可以放宽很多约束,比如编写代码是免费的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Okay, so that's neat.
zh: 好的,这很整洁。

speaker: Unknown
en: With that in mind, what do you want to do?
zh: 考虑到这一点,你想做什么?

speaker: Unknown
en: What would be best suited for the language, the compiler for testing, for self-reflection, for supervisor models, all these things.
zh: 什么将最适合于语言、编译器、用于测试、用于自我反思、用于监督模型、所有这些东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think that's more of a programming system than a language, but I think when we create something like that, it can really enable creators, builders to create incredibly robust, incredibly complex systems.
zh: 我认为这更像是一个编程系统而不是一门语言,但我认为当我们创造出这样的东西时,它真的可以赋予创作者、构建者创造极其鲁棒、极其复杂的系统的能力。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I'm super excited about VibeCoding, but I don't know generating a prototype has been the limiting factor in software ever.
zh: 我对 VibeCoding 感到超级兴奋,但我不知道生成原型是否一直是软件中的制约因素。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's actually building increasingly complex systems and actually changing them with agility.
zh: 实际上构建日益复杂的系统并以敏捷性改变它们才是。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you look at the famous Netscape one to Netscape two rewrite, somewhat, a lot of people attribute that to part of their failure against Internet Explorer.
zh: 如果你看看著名的从 Netscape 1 到 Netscape 2 的重写,某种程度上,很多人将其归因于他们对抗 Internet Explorer 失败的部分原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's like making these things is not hard.
zh: 这就像制造这些东西并不难。

speaker: Unknown
en: Maintaining them is hard and ensuring they're robust is hard.
zh: 维护它们是困难的,确保它们鲁棒是困难的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think we're in the very early phases of defining what this new system for developing software looks like and I'm very excited to see what emerges.
zh: 我认为我们正处于定义这个软件开发新系统样貌的非常早期阶段,我很兴奋能看到什么会涌现出来。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like we're definitely living in the future when someone like you is suggesting that we build a matrix like experience and that's going to be potentially the future of coding and building.
zh: 我觉得当像你这样的人建议我们构建一个像《黑客帝国》那样的体验,并且那可能是编码和构建的未来时,我们绝对生活在未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: I can't wait for that.
zh: 我迫不及待了。

speaker: Unknown
en: It feels like a great opportunity and a fun project.
zh: 这感觉像是一个很好的机会和一个有趣的项目。

en: Big fan of the podcast and the newsletter.

en: Vanta is a long time sponsor of the show, but for some of our newer listeners, what does Vanta do and who is it for?
zh: Vanta 是我们节目长期的赞助商，但对于我们的一些新听众来说，Vanta 是做什么的，它是为谁服务的？

en: So we started Vanta in 2018 focused on founders helping them start to build out their security programs and get credit for all of that hard security work with compliance certifications like SOC 2 or ISO 2701.

en: Today, we currently help over 9,000 companies including some start-up household names like Atlassian Ramp and LangChain, start and scale their security programs and ultimately, build trust by automating compliance, centralizing GRC, and accelerating security reviews.
zh: 如今，我们帮助超过 9000 家公司，包括一些像 Atlassian、Ramp 和 LangChain 这样的知名初创公司，启动和扩展他们的安全计划，并通过自动化合规、集中化 GRC 和加速安全审查，最终建立信任。

en: That is awesome.

en: I know from experience that these things take a lot of time and a lot of resources and nobody wants to spend time doing this.
zh: 根据我的经验，这些事情需要花费大量的时间和资源，没有人愿意花时间做这些。

en: That is very much our experience, but before the company and to some extent, during it.
zh: 这也是我们的深刻体会，无论是在公司成立之前，还是在某种程度上在公司成立之后。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the idea is with automation, with AI, with software, we are helping customers build trust with prospects and customers in an efficient way.
zh: 但我们的理念是，通过自动化、通过 AI、通过软件，我们帮助客户以高效的方式与潜在客户和现有客户建立信任。

speaker: Unknown
en: And our joke, we started this compliance company so you don't have to.
zh: 我们常开玩笑说，我们创立这家合规公司就是为了你们不必自己去建立合规体系。

en: We appreciate you for doing that.
zh: 我们感谢你这样做。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks for that, Christina.
zh: 谢谢你，Christina。
